conclusion.justification: The report concludes that high-quality evidence is inconclusive and insufficient to determine whether hypnosis helps with smoking cessation, explicitly noting that while it is not proven more effective than other options, it is also not proven ineffective.
conclusion.label: hedged

report:
The evidence does **not** clearly support the claim that hypnosis helps with smoking cessation—current high-quality research is inconclusive rather than affirmatively positive.

The most authoritative source is the Cochrane systematic review (Barnes et al., 2019), which analyzed 14 randomized controlled trials involving 1,926 participants. It concluded there is "insufficient evidence to determine whether hypnotherapy is more effective for smoking cessation than other forms of behavioural support or unassisted quitting" (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001008_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking). The review rated study quality poorly: only one trial was judged low risk of bias, while 10 were high risk and three unclear, and most individual studies found no statistically significant benefit (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6568235).

A more recent meta-analysis (Frontiers, 2023) examined five reviews, including three Cochrane reviews, and found effect sizes ranging from d=0.12 to 0.84 across six comparisons—but only two of those effects reached statistical significance, reinforcing the picture of weak, inconsistent evidence (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1330238/full).

Some individual trials, such as those comparing hypnotherapy to nicotine replacement therapy, have reported favorable results, and a 2025 broader review (Ekanayake and Elkins) covering 63 studies reported more positive support (https://www.ishhypnosis.org/encyclopedia/the-potential-benefit-of-hypnosis-for-smoking-cessation/). However, these findings conflict with the rigorous, bias-controlled Cochrane synthesis.

**Bottom line:** The claim that hypnosis definitively helps smoking cessation is not well supported. The best available evidence (Cochrane) indicates uncertainty—hypnotherapy is not proven more effective than other behavioral approaches or quitting unassisted, though it isn't proven ineffective either. More rigorous, low-bias trials are needed before drawing firm conclusions.
